doc.title: Ken Peplowski interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 10, 1997 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Disliking contemporary pop-jazz; memorable tunes
summary: He dislikes calculated pop-jazz, praises the Crusaders, and they joke about hummable themes.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Yeah, well maybe in a way. But the amazing thing, with all those changes is that people still — musicians and listeners can be very closed minded and say I just like music of the 1930s, I just like to listen to Coltrane and beyond. There’s so much out there that you could listen to and love and why limit yourself to one small little gap of time? So I really try to play and listen to as many things as I can. And even if I’m playing an old standard, somehow all these things are filtered into my playing. For me, if I play a song that’s written in 1920, I’m not thinking of trying to re-create some old style or play like Benny Goodman or do something like that. This is me, and this is a song I like, and this is what I’m playing, although I loved Benny. And as far as contemporary jazz or Kenny G type stuff, that music I dislike in the same way that I dislike manufactured calculated pop music. It’s the same thing. It’s almost like it’s music made by a committee. It’s just boring to me. Electric drums and like the fake soul filigrees that they play on every tune. Some of those kind of groups — I used to love The Crusaders for example, because they were very creative within that kind of music. They were playing together, they were improvising together.
Yeah, in my opinion when a Crusaders tune was done, you could hum the tune back.
You know, sometimes when I listen to some of the more contemporary guys, when the tune is over it’s like, hmmm, how did that go?

That’s right. In fact Steve Allen, you know the piano player? He was telling me, he was talking about this very thing. And he said, “I defy you to hum back the tune to the new Tonight Show.” I can’t think of it.
That’s true. And you see that in some of the T.V. shows too. You know I bet if I asked you, you could hum the tune to The Dick VanDyke Show.
Of course, all those old things, yeah.
You know, N.Y.P.D. Blue has cool theme but it’s not like, hmmm, yeah, oh there’s a drum thing and, you know.
